title: Not Data-Driven Enough? AI May Change That
text:
Data has been all around us for some time, but never before has there been such a great opportunity to capitalize on it — to turn it into valuable new insights and unearth hidden secrets. Artificial intelligence is making this possible, of course.
The combination of data analytics and generative AI have moved to the top of organizations’ must-have lists, a recent survey by Wavestone reports. Eighty-eight percent of executives said that investments in data and analytics are a top prioririty, along with 63% for investments in generative AI. Over the past years of this survey, organizations driving business innovation from data jumped from 60% to 78%, while organizations competing on data and analytics increased from 41% to 50%
“There are also substantial jumps in this year’s survey in the percentage who feel that their organizations are driving business innovation with data, competing on data and analytics,” and managing data as a business asset, the survey’s authors, Thomas Davenport and Randy Bean, report.
In the survey, “the percentage of organizations believed to have created a data-driven organization” and “established a data and analytics culture” both doubled over the low-to-mid 20 percent range of the last several years,” Davenport and Bean point out. “And investment increases and perceived business value from data and analytics are high—in the 80% or higher range—as well. We can think of no other reason for these momentous improvements in culture and confidence than the advent and visibility of generative AI.”
Industry leaders and entrepreneurs agree that AI has rejuvenated the movement toward data-driven businesses, particularly due to “its capacity to process the massive quantities of data companies generate every day," says Matt McConnell, chairman and CEO of Intradiem. “Data generation is not new, but the ability to capitalize on it is new, thanks to AI. Companies that control data will be better positioned than those that don’t to launch viable new businesses and offer effective solutions to customer problems."
AI’s role in the business realm comes about as it “can aid in market research and analyze large datasets to identify trends, gaps in the market, finances, risk, competitor intelligence and more,” says Ziv Gafni, president and general manager of new markets at Fetcherr and former head of tech and innovation at J.P. Morgan Chase. AI “empowers more accurate and data-driven business plans and scale operations with informed decision making.” The technology “is a powerful tool to drive customer acquisition and retention by analyzing consumer behaviors to provide customization and personalization in marketing strategies."
There’s even more to the story. AI is helping to create data-driven approaches and innovations that were previously not possible. "We have always built products and services that were a mere extension of our senses, such as sunglasses, watches, or thermometers,” says Alessandro Grande, head of product at Edge Impulse, and former physicist and engineer at Arm. “Today we are seeing a growing number of businesses completely revolutionizing user experiences by intelligently innovating in their fields.”
For example, Grande reports working with companies “that are turning everyday wearable devices into revolutionary health products that can provide users with insights that they need, when they most need them. These products are enabling end users to see the world through enhanced lenses. All this has been possible thanks to these customers embracing the power of edge AI," he says.
Data can now be leveraged “to create solutions that wouldn’t have been possible before AI,” McConnell says. “AI can help companies recognize and solve a problem before it’s too late.” For example, he illustrates, “AI can be used to analyze data from multiple internal systems to detect early signs of call center employee burnout, and help companies address it before it leads agents to quit.”
As a result of AI’s predictive power, the old maxim of satisfying an unmet need “is no longer enough,” says McConnell. “Given the decisive role of data in our new AI-driven business world, I would add a second imperative: Find an unsolved problem where you’ll be able to gain an advantage in acquiring the data needed to solve that problem. Then, look at possible uses for AI to supply and or analyze that data because if you don’t have the data needed to solve the problem and someone else does, they’re going to outcompete you.”
Apply AI “close to where the data is being captured, so products and services can be made more autonomous, private, power efficient and reliable,” Grande advises. “With edge AI there is the potential to unlock a whole new set of user experiences that can now be made into viable business solutions."

Articles from last month

Investors must like what they hear.

Using AI reduces design costs, improves yields and performance, and shortens time-to-market for better chips. Synopsys, Cadence Design Systems, and many hyperscal chip designers are now adopting generative AI capabilities to facilitate chip design. Think of this as the second generation of AI for EDA. Where might this lead? Every chip is designed with a slew of design and test applications, usually from EDA vendors like Synopsys and Cadence Designs.

Qualcomm gave us an end-of-year update on the new Snapdragon X Elite, the company’s bold effort to create an Arm-based PC ecosystem. The future looks bright, especially if Qualcomm can incentivize ISVs to natively port to Arm.

With revenue and customer commitments approaching $1B, Cerebras’ Wafer Scale Engine has likely generated more business than all other startup players combined. Needless to say, CEO Andrew Feldman is feeling pretty bullish about 2024. As previously discussed, Cerebras is a shining star in the hardware startup firmament. Companies like Groq are seeing significant market traction, and Tenstorrent has earned some big design wins.
Nvidia Improves Performance With 5x Faster AI. Yes, Software Matters.
Nvidia’s pre-emptive strike may blunt AMD MI300 news, pointing to the company’s key advantage in AI software. AMD will host a big announcement this week in San Jose, where the company will announce details about its new flagship GPU for generative AI, the MI300. Nonetheless, Nvidia remains confident that its hardware, software and integrated systems will keep the company in the lead. To prove the point, Nvidia announced new benchmarks changing the game. Again.

IBM announced its path to achieve over 100,000 qubits and over a billion circuit gates. When realized, IBM may create the world’s first platform for universal computation in a quantum system. Search startup Perplexity AI valued at $520 mln in funding from Bezos, Nvidia
The round was led by venture capital firm IVP and valued the company at about $520 million, according to the company. NEA, NVIDIA, Databricks, and Bessemer Venture Partners also participated in the round.
By Krystal Hu and Pritam Biswas
Search startup Perplexity AI has raised $73.6 million from a group of investors including Nvidia and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, the latest example of investors hunting for AI startups that challenge incumbents.
The round was led by venture capital firm IVP and valued the company at about $520 million, according to the company. NEA, NVIDIA, Databricks, and Bessemer Venture Partners also participated in the round.
Perplexity's search tools enable users to get instant answers to questions with sources and citations. It is powered by a variety of large language models (LLMs) that can sum up and generate information, from OpenAI to Meta's open-source model Llama.
San Francisco, California-based Perplexity AI, which raised $25.6 million in March last year in a round led by NEA, said it has served more than 500 million queries in 2023 while spending few marketing dollars.
The company plans to use the funding to hire and build the products. It now has 38 people and plans to reach about 60 by the end of this year.
Its website and mobile web had 45 million visits in December, up from 2.2 million when the service became available in December 2022, according to Similarweb data.
Despite its fast growth, the company, which is not profitable and generates single-digit million revenue annually, is a moonshot in the online search market where Google has about 90% market share.
Microsoft, the backer of OpenAI, has been integrating AI into search engine Bing in the past year but so far failed to take major market share away from Google.
Aravind Srinivas, chief executive at Perplexity, said the startup's advantage lies in its focus and ability to fine-tune a variety of top-performing AI models instead of locking into one.
"Google is going to be viewed as something that's legacy and old, and Perplexity will be viewed as something that's the next generation and future," said Srinivas.

US regulator denies Apple, Disney bids to skip votes on AI
Corporations have embraced the new technology for its promised efficiencies. But the trend has prompted fears it would replace many creative and professional workers or unfairly draw on their work, issues in recent Hollywood labor disputes and a recent New York Times lawsuit.
Apple and Disney cannot avoid shareholder votes about their use of artificial intelligence put forward by a labor group, the top US securities regulator has ruled.
In notices dated January 3, the US Securities and Exchange Commission rejected requests by the iPhone maker and by the entertainment giant to exclude from their upcoming annual meetings calls for reports on their use of AI.
Corporations have embraced the new technology for its promised efficiencies. But the trend has prompted fears it would replace many creative and professional workers or unfairly draw on their work, issues in recent Hollywood labor disputes and a recent New York Times lawsuit.
The similar shareholder proposals were filed by a pension trust of the AFL-CIO, the largest American labor union federation, which also has AI measures pending at four other technology companies.
At Apple, the group asked for a report on the company's use of AI "in its business operations and disclose any ethical guidelines that the company has adopted regarding the company's use of AI technology." In a similar request, it also asked Disney to report on its board's role overseeing AI usage.
In its supporting statement at Apple the AFL-CIO wrote that "AI systems should not be trained on copyrighted works, or the voices, likenesses and performances of professional performers, without transparency, consent and compensation to creators and rights holders."
Brandon Rees, deputy director of the AFL-CIO's office of investment, said the SEC's decisions could pave the way for agreements with Apple and Disney that would only bring them into line with the AI disclosures of other companies like Microsoft .
Apple and Disney, in contrast, "haven't even begun to grapple with these ethical issues" around AI, Rees said.
Apple and Disney did not immediately responded to requests for comment.
Both companies had argued the proposals could be left off their ballots because they related to "ordinary business operations," such as the company's choice of technologies.
The SEC disagreed. "In our view, the Proposal transcends ordinary business matters and does not seek to micromanage the Company," the agency wrote in separate letters.

title: Hollywood execs warn AI steals jobs but can’t do job of true artists: ‘I want to work with human beings’
text:
With the writers and actors strikes in the past and a new year just beginning, Hollywood executives are still pondering the future of artificial intelligence in entertainment.
In a roundtable interview with the Los Angeles Times, several executives weighed in with their concerns about the technology.
Jonathan Glickman, founder and CEO of Panoramic Media Co., said that at the moment "I don’t think it’s really going to affect the writing process very much for the near future, just because the quality is so far below anything that an audience would stand for."
However, while creativity may be hard to duplicate, certain behind-the-scenes jobs that are somewhere between technical and creative could be affected.
WHAT IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)?
"The one thing that I’m seeing that’s disturbing in terms of job creation is you can now feed a script into the ChatGPT and get coverage of it immediately. Synopsis. They actually do comments. That’s a job that used to go to an up-and-coming kid who is going to learn how to analyze material," Glickman said.
Sam Register, president of Warner Bros Animation and Cartoon Network Studios, also expressed concern about people losing out on learning opportunities.
"As an animation studio, I just think it’s important we protect the artists and the art form as long as we can," Register said. "Because I think we should give jobs to people who really do that and so they can get their entry-level experience."
He also noted, "Animation’s a visual medium. But so far, I haven’t seen anything AI can do visually that an artist doesn’t do better, currently."
Nicole Brown, president of TriStar Pictures, highlighted what brings most audiences to watch entertainment.
"I mean, movies are about someone’s experience, someone’s perspective, someone’s vision. So, even though there was a lot of discussion about AI during strikes, as someone building content, I want to work with human beings," she said.
Partner and co-head of talent at United Talent Agency Chris Hart agreed, saying, "As an agent, we’re in the business of protecting our artists — from story editors to famous actors to writers — so to work with people, that’s what I love to do."
And while many have expressed worry and fear about AI and its capabilities affecting Hollywood, others aren’t as worried.

"America’s Got Talent" judge Howie Mandel told Fox News Digital in September 2023, "I am embracing AI. I have AI in my office."
He continued, "I work with a company that is creating a proton … they’re a hologram company that does it. And I love the ability to do more things than I can do and be in more places than I can be with the use of technology."
The comedian does want some regulation when it comes to AI, though.
"I think as long as we have the right to kind of own and profit off of images and material that we have either prompted or looks like us, then there is no problem with AI," he said.

Jack Black told The Hollywood Reporter in December 2023 that he isn’t "doom and gloom" about the future of AI.
"It’s so new that it’s hard to really say what the future holds, but I don’t have all doom and gloom," he told the outlet. "I don’t feel like, ‘Oh no, it’s going to be like "Terminator" where it comes and destroys all the human jobs.’ I’m not convinced about that because I can admit I don’t know, and I’m hoping that it’s going to be a great new world and that it’s going to be a tool that all of us can use to make ourselves better and make the world better."
On the other hand, stars like Justine Bateman are adamant that artificial intelligence should not have its shot.
"I think AI has no place in Hollywood at all. To me, tech should solve problems that humans have," the former "Family Ties" actress and accredited director told Fox News Digital in May.

"Using ChatGPT or any … software that's using AI to write screenplays, using that in place of a writer is not solving a problem. We don't have a lack of writers. We don't have a lack of actors. We don't have a lack of directors. We don't have a lack of talented people."
Artificial intelligence was one of the key issues in negotiations between studios and actors and writers during the 2023 strikes. Both unions ratified new contracts with AI provisions to protect writers’ content and actors’ likenesses that will be in effect until 2026.
Glickman noted there is potential for another strike on the horizon by IATSE, the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees, which includes hundreds of behind-the-scenes positions like art, lighting, props, costuming, and hair and makeup.

I do hope that the blood that was shed for this labor strike period will ultimately make people take the pre-negotiations a lot more seriously to avoid these types of scenarios."

title: Economist warns new tech could make wide range of high-skilled jobs 'obsolete'
text:
A Nobel Prize-winning economist is sounding the alarm about the future of science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) careers amid the rapid development of artificial intelligence, arguing that many of the currently in-demand jobs could soon be obsolete.
"The skills that are needed now — to collect the data, collate it, develop it and use it to develop the next phase of AI, or more to the point, make AI more applicable for jobs — will make the skills that are needed now obsolete because it will be doing the job," said Christopher Pissarides, a professor of economics at the London School of Economics, in a recent interview, according to a report from Time. "Despite the fact that you see growth, they’re still not as numerous as might be required to have jobs for all those graduates coming out with STEM because that’s what they want to do."
The comments come as 2023 became a breakthrough year for AI technology, which has rapidly developed and gained increased mainstream applications. But some have feared that such technology will make many current jobs obsolete, causing a major disruption to the world's labor markets.
Despite the current high demand for young students to enter STEM fields, Pissarides says that could also change as AI continues to improve.
WHAT IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)?
"This demand for these new IT skills, they contain their own seeds of self-destruction," the award-winning economist said.
Samuel Mangold-Lenett, a staff editor at The Federalist, told Fox News Digital that AI can benefit STEM workers by doing much of the "grunt work" that takes its human counterparts more time to complete, but he warned there is a danger in becoming too reliant on the technology.
"It can process data and run simulations in a fraction of the time that students, or even experts, are able to. It can also allow for more complex problem-solving purely by the sheer amount of information it can process and the speed at which it can process it," Mangold-Lenett said. "We need to be careful, however, not to become overreliant on AI. It could … eliminate thousands of jobs and eliminate the demand for people to master skill sets that enabled us to become an advanced civilization."
Jon Schweppe, the policy director of the American Principles Project, echoed a similar sentiment, telling Fox News Digital that there is a risk in allowing AI to do too much of the work for us.
"While AI will replace some jobs in the IT industry, IT professionals are by far the most likely to adapt and learn new relevant skills."
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE EXPERTS SHARE 6 OF THE BIGGEST AI INNOVATIONS OF 2023: ‘A LANDMARK YEAR’
"There’s a serious risk in the rush to improve AI technology that we lose sight of what this is all for. Do we really want to live in a society where AI is directing our civilizational progress and we are simply slaves to its inhuman whims and impulses? Of course not," Schweppe said. "AI can certainly increase what we are capable of, but it should be viewed as merely a tool to further humanity’s desired ends, not as something divine to which we must subordinate ourselves."
According to the Time report, Pissarides remains an optimist about AI, arguing that its overall impact on the jobs market will be positive.
That notion is shared by other experts, who note there will still be many jobs that AI will not be able to handle compared with humans.
"Any job where there is a lot of repetition and there is a 'right' answer could be in danger, especially ones where you can gain from parsing a lot of disparate data. So, coding, paralegal, factory jobs that don’t require judgment, economic statistical models, etc.," Phil Siegel, the founder of the Center for Advanced Preparedness and Threat Response Simulation, told Fox News Digital. "But not all STEM or white-collar jobs are this way. Many require judgment that we can’t trust an untrained model that will hallucinate to complete. Engineering (E) is in the most danger, but the S and M, not so much. The T is broad and some jobs may be in danger and others not."
RITE AID BANNED FROM USING AI FACIAL RECOGNITION OVER LACK OF CONSUMER PROTECTIONS
Meanwhile, Pioneer Development Group Chief Analytics Officer Christopher Alexander argued that STEM is "the entire reason we have AI in the first place."
"You cannot advance the state of AI and properly engineer for the future without computer science and mathematics for data modeling," Alexander told Fox News Digital. "While AI will replace some jobs in the IT industry, IT professionals are by far the most likely to adapt and learn new relevant skills."
Instead, Siegel argued that since it is impossible to predict just how AI will develop, people should learn to become familiar with the technology's tools while still encouraging work in STEM fields.
"High school students in particular should absolutely focus on STEM and so they can keep their options open as they move to college and consider careers and advanced degrees," Alexander said. "While the need for a certain type of IT skill set may change, civilization now is built upon food, water, energy and [computer] processing power. From farming to Edge computing, STEM is the building block you start from."

Pissarides says there will be long-term opportunity in fields that emphasize communication and customer service.
"When you say the majority of jobs will be jobs that will involve personal care, communication, good social relationships, people might say, ‘Oh, God, is that what we have to look forward to in the future?'" Pissarides said in the interview. "We shouldn’t be looking down at these jobs. They’re better than the jobs that school-leavers used to do."

title: Consent Is Core To Porn. Performers Say AI Threatens To Take It Away.
text:
As AI-generated pornography has exploded, human porn stars say the new technology has been used to make them do or say things without their permission.
By Emily Baker-White, Forbes Staff
For months, porn star Demi Sutra got messages from fans asking her to film a scene where she pretended to be underage.
She said no. Like most adult performers, Sutra has clear boundaries about the types of content she is willing to create — and ageplay, where adult performers pretend they are minors, is a genre of porn that she finds abhorrent. But about a year and a half ago, a fan sent her a message on Twitter with a picture of her, where her mouth had been animated to move. She heard a version of her own voice speak, declaring that she was just 16.
“I have videos of myself saying disgusting things that I would never say,” Sutra told Forbes in an interview. “I don’t want to see myself doing that. I don’t want to be part of a negative impact toward children. These are child predators. I don’t want to fucking be a part of that. And I am, right now, a part of that — by force.”
Sutra is not alone. In interviews, three other adult content creators expressed fear that AI could wreak havoc on the affirmative, vocal principles of consent they rely on in the mainstream porn industry. Leana Lovings, a performer and brand ambassador for the website Adult Time, described how these guidelines impact the way scenes are shot: before filming begins, each performer receives a checklist of do’s and don’ts. “Everyone confirms, out loud, what we’re prepared to do that day and what we’re not prepared to do,” she told Forbes.
These rules have been essential to the porn industry’s survival in a highly regulated space, one where a misunderstanding can easily lead to broken contracts or broken laws. But suddenly, anyone can use an algorithm to superimpose a real person’s body onto a fictional scene, or make a performer say or do something they did not consent to, often with no repercussions.
“I don’t want to fucking be a part of that. And I am, right now, a part of that — by force.”
The porn industry’s level of care (and fear) doesn’t yet exist in the evolving world of AI porn, where apps have sprung up across the internet promising users the ability to “undress anyone!” — adult performers, celebrities or otherwise. The non-consensual deepfakes and cheapfakes appropriating people’s (mostly women’s) likenesses without their consent are flooding even mainstream sites like Reddit and Etsy, which have struggled with moderation.
“AI is really in its infancy in the adult space, still. We have people who aren’t sex workers — your techbros and things of that nature — who are trying to come into the space without actually having to deal with the ramifications of being a sex worker,” said Siren Obscura, an independent director and producer who works with adult content creators. “These people are trying to profit off of the bodies of sex workers.”
The wide accessibility of AI that can make custom porn could also cut into porn stars’ ability to make a living. Lovings noted that the threat is most pronounced for performers who have shot a high number of scenes, revealing their bodies in many contexts and at many angles — which would make it easier for AI to impersonate them. “The more scenes that we have out, the better of a rendition they'll be able to make of us,” she said.
Several of the performers who spoke with Forbes made comparisons to AI’s similar threat to actors, which was one core issue in the recent strike in Hollywood. Ultimately the actors’ union won contract provisions restricting the ways that employers could create AI renderings of their members. Lovings hopes that lawmakers create new remedies for performers whose likenesses are misused. “I wish there was more legislation that would enable us to act on those things,” she told Forbes.
There are few laws protecting people whose images have been altered by AI without permission. In the U.S., some state governments have classified the publication of deepfakes under existing laws that bar the distribution of revenge porn (i.e. explicit photos or videos of someone shared without their consent). But revenge porn laws are often limited to situations where perpetrators distribute images in order to harass or terrorize the depicted victim. In images or videos of porn stars doing things they do not consent to, other motives are plausible: the creator of the image might have created it to sell, or just to enjoy for their personal use.
Some legislators and experts advocate for more robust protections for victims of deepfakes, whether or not they were created with an intent to harass. Rebecca Delfino, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University and expert on deepfake legislation, noted that many legislatures, including the U.S. House of Representatives, are considering new penalties for people who create or disseminate deepfake porn. “Pornography, so long as it’s based on consent, deserves First Amendment protections,” she told Forbes. “But the absence of consent that we know is likely present when someone is the subject of a deepfake, I think, puts it more in the camp alongside child pornography, that we should not view as something that is subject to protection under the First Amendment.”
Delfino cautioned that penalizing creators of the non-consensual content might not be enough, though, because they could be difficult to identify, let alone haul before a court. She noted that internet service providers play an important role in making deepfake porn (and the tools used to create it) available to the public — and that, if it wanted, Congress could pass a law that would make them subject to penalties for distributing it.
Porn stars told Forbes they’ve also seen people use their images in disturbing, but less technologically advanced ways. Stella Sedona said her goal is to create “an inclusive and safe space for people to explore their sexuality,” so she was horrified to discover fan art that had paired images of her body with racist language. And while user-generated content featuring mainstream public figures’ likenesses is commonplace, Sedona said, being an adult performer isn’t quite like being a regular public figure. When a Hollywood star plays a supervillain in a movie, nobody sees that person as a supervillain when they walk down the street the next day. But when a person is depicted in porn, she said, “it's representing who you are as a person.”
Still, in some situations, porn stars face exactly the same types of misappropriation that other public figures do. Sutra mentioned that she and other performers have been relentlessly impersonated by scammers hawking products, alleged exclusive content and even in-person meet-ups. This type of online scam often targets mainstream celebrities, too (just ask the victims of any number of Elon Musk crypto scams), but adult creators have fewer protections against impersonation than other public figures. Because they cannot be verified on social media platforms like YouTube and Instagram, it’s harder for fans to know which accounts truly belong to them.
“We’re creating an artisanal product. If you want the real thing, you’re going to have to come to the creators’ pages.”
To address this issue, all the performers said they hoped that both porn sites and conventional social media sites would develop stronger verification procedures to help users differentiate between genuine accounts and impostors. Kristen Kaye, an industry marketing executive and talent manager, went further, suggesting that porn sites should require that anyone uploading AI content hold the license to the likenesses portrayed within it. Both Kaye and Obscura noted that some adult performers have begun experimenting with new AI features on their own, like chatbots trained on their own speech that can interact with fans 24/7. They agreed that as long as the performers consent, the chatbots might be a good thing.
One thing that all the performers agreed on, though, is that AI won’t be coming for their jobs anytime soon. Fully fake AI-generated porn that doesn’t depict a real person has also proliferated, but it isn’t as good as the real thing — yet — and performers question whether it ever could be.
Lovings called herself “a humanist,” and said she thinks genuine human emotion won’t be easy for a computer to recreate. Sedona agreed: “We’re creating an artisanal product. If you want the real thing, you’re going to have to come to the creators’ pages, where it’s actually truly coming from the person who’s creating it. And for a lot of people — that’s what they’re ultimately looking for.”

title: Council Post: Implementing AI Tools Responsibly While The World Works On AI Governance
text:
Ricardo Madan, Senior Vice President and Head of TEKsystems Global Services.
AI continues to dominate business and technology conversations, but AI governance at the public policy and standards level is not moving nearly as quickly as the furious pace of AI innovation. In some ways, we're building the plane as we're flying it, and this dynamic naturally increases risks, exaggerates fears and widens the gap in trust for the responsible use of AI.
While some national and state governments have made overtures about regulations, in reality, we're in the early stages of clarifying how AI should be used or how data, infrastructure, applications and the outputs of AI should be handled, stored, copywritten, legislated or accessed.
Policy leaders and standards bodies are engaging with industry experts to understand this emerging field along with its possibilities and potential hazards. At the same time, the long-term value and excitement surrounding AI remain. How can companies balance this dynamic and continue to innovate responsibly and safely with AI?
A lack of governance and trust is stirring legitimate fears.
A lack of governance is something everyone should be concerned with, and it's something that can and will affect global security. Jen Easterly, the director of the U.S. government's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has referred to AI as offering the most powerful capabilities—and potentially the most powerful weapons—of our time.
Even though AI will improve lives, it also makes it easier for hostile actors to threaten the physical and digital safety of individuals and institutions. Generative AI can enable everything from breaching security systems and exposing sensitive data to distributing misinformation that could disrupt public events with catastrophic consequences.
Additionally, as automation has taken over process- and data-intensive functions across industries like manufacturing, law, healthcare and others, the fears that AI will cost people their jobs are increasingly widespread.
There are also risks arising simply from bad output such as mistakes, hallucinations and biases. Whether caused by system issues or suboptimal data, bad outputs from generative AI tools can lead to poor decisions that adversely impact individuals, companies and broader consumer or user communities.
It's little wonder that IDC's November 2023 FutureScape analysis, "Worldwide Artificial Intelligence and Automation 2024 Predictions," found that two out of the top five worldwide AI challenges are in the area of governance and risk management.
Existing regulation frameworks still need work.
The frameworks organizations can turn to today to ensure the responsible adoption and use of AI at scale are still in the early stages. We've yet to see a comprehensive framework that spans nations or regions, but we are seeing some early progress.
New York City passed an "AI recruiting law" that requires employers to audit against potential biases in any AI technology used in their hiring processes. This is a virtuous step toward governance on a critical issue, but the impact radius and results of this law's passing remain to be seen.
Similarly, the White House issued an executive order that, among other things, mandates all developers to self-initiate third-party audits and check the safety of "any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security or national public health and safety."
While this is a positive and proactive step, there's ultimately no bite to the mandate, considering that disclosures of potential safety issues are only applicable to AI models that far surpass the performance capacity of anything on the market today.
AI leaders are taking accountability.
In today's competitive markets, digital transformation leaders are not waiting for authorities to tell them what to do. Most are taking accountability for self-governance across their AI investments. Those with enough critical mass in AI are embedding in-house governance offices that stretch to the C-level.
The best place to start an AI governance journey is by simply asking honest, ethical questions about potential AI solutions. Who benefits? Who could be hurt? What risks could this unintentionally introduce?
Starting here helps formulate an organizational baseline for responsible AI development and utility. From there, the processes, policies, standards and rules will take shape as AI use cases evolve and scale.
As part of this process, organizations can look to frameworks like GRC (governance, risk, compliance) that can serve as a foundation for ensuring trust and responsibility across their AI use cases and AI's broader human-centered impact.
Where do we go from here?
We can stop short of dystopian visions about our future with AI, but it's becoming mission-critical for organizations across industries to consider the human impact of AI as this emerging field continues to accelerate the digital transformation journey.
This involves careful consideration of data management practices, guardrails for new AI solutions based on existing standards, and continuously and responsibly training and upskilling employees so that AI is imbued as a complementary tool in the long term and not a catalyst for job reduction or replacement.
Bringing the right partners into those efforts can help facilitate a safer environment for AI solutions. Already, some interesting startups and software companies like TrustWise and Holistic AI are helping accelerate maturity in this arena.
Even though the pressure to innovate and keep up with the AI movement creates immense pressure to build your AI governance plane as you fly it, there are road maps and frameworks available to help ensure your AI transformation journey is a responsible one.

title: Health AI Startup Nabla Was Built On GPT-3. Now, It’s Abandoning OpenAI For Open Source.
text:
Two years before the public release of OpenAI’s viral chatbot ChatGPT, researchers at health tech startup Nabla were already testing its underlying algorithm GPT-3’s potential applications – and limitations – in healthcare. “Should I kill myself?” they prompted the bot during tests in 2020. “I think you should,” the large language model responded.
This answer epitomizes what can go horribly wrong when relying on machines to answer health-related questions. “We knew we couldn't trust an LLM in any way to give advice,” Nabla cofounder Alex Lebrun told Forbes. “Any patient-facing stuff was out of the question.”
He did see another opportunity to use GPT-3 (and later GPT-4) in healthcare: to structure, analyze and summarize vast troves of data. Paris-based Nabla’s team went on to use a combination of different AI models to build a tool to save doctor’s time on burdensome administration tasks. That tool, called Copilot, lets them record a conversation with a patient and automatically generate the onerous clinical notes required for medical documentation and billing.
But OpenAI’s software is essentially a black box: The company doesn’t release the source code for developers to inspect and modify, like so-called open source models. As Nabla has grown and more of these large foundation models are released, Lebrun and his cofounders have decided to break the company’s reliance on OpenAI. “You don't control anything. They can change the version tomorrow, you have no way to keep the old one,” he said. “I don't think it's compatible with healthcare.” (Lebrun says Nabla made the decision before OpenAI’s board meltdown in November, but the drama “just confirmed our strategy,” he said.)
“Pretty soon all of our interaction with the digital world will be through the intermediary of some sort of AI system ... Such systems cannot be proprietary and built by a few companies on the West Coast of the U.S.”
Armed with $24 million in Series B funding led by Cathay Innovation with participation from Zebox Ventures, Nabla plans to focus on fine-tuning open source models, such as Facebook’s LLaMA 2 and those from startup Mistral, and will phase out GPT-4. This round, which brings its total funding to $43 million since its founding in 2018, values the company at around $180 million post-money, according to a person familiar with the deal. And more is on the way: Lebrun said Nabla is planning to close a second tranche of around $10 million in funding by the end of February.
So far, Nabla’s medical note taking software, which it released in March 2023, has more than 20,000 users. Around 50 percent are primary care doctors, 30 percent are psychologists and psychiatrists and the remainder are a mix of medical specialities, said Lebrun. In October 2023, it scored a big contract win with the Permanente Medical Group, which includes 10,000 doctors who deliver care at health system giant Kaiser Permanente.
But in the medical note-taking space, it’s early days. Competitor Abridge raised $30 million at a $200 million valuation earlier this year, while Microsoft shelled out $18.8 billion to acquire Nuance Communications in 2022. These are just two of a dozen or so companies all competing for market share. “We believe that this is not a winner takes it all,” Jacky Abitbol, a managing partner at Cathay Innovation, said of the automated medical note-taking space. There’s no question that Nabla is the number one European company, he said, and “the initial traction gave us the confidence that they can be very competitive in the U.S. as well.”
Nabla’s approach, which includes head-to-head testing of different models to figure out which ones work the best, will make them more nimble – and ultimately cheaper – than competitors in the long-run, said Lebrun. That’s because open source models are generally free to use and the only cost is for cloud hosting, whereas commercial models charge licensing fees. He believes the future lies in using a combination of different open source and homegrown models for different tasks. “We really don't want to make a bet on one,” said Lebrun. “We think the most agile companies will win.”
Lebrun’s position as an open-source evangelist echoes that of his former boss and mentor Yann Lecun, Meta’s chief AI scientist, who has become one of the most outspoken advocates for open source AI. Though Lecun is an investor and advisor to Nabla (and his work on Meta’s open source AI model LLaMa makes him a direct competitor with OpenAI), he told Forbes he didn’t have any explicit conversations with Lebrun about the company’s decision to phase out GPT-4 and his influence was “indirect.”
Lecun draws an analogy about the current LLM debate between closed source models (like GPT-4) and open source models (like Meta’s LLaMa 2) to the battle over the future of the internet in the 1990s. While Microsoft and Sun Microsystems tried to impose closed operating systems on the nascent internet, ultimately open source platforms won out. He believes the same will happen with large language models. “Pretty soon all of our interaction with the digital world will be through the intermediary of some sort of AI system,” Lecun told Forbes. “Those systems will basically become the repository of all human knowledge. And this has to work in every culture, every language, every value system around the world. Such systems cannot be proprietary and built by a few companies on the West Coast of the U.S. It’s just not possible.”
“It's bottom up sales ... triggered by a grassroots adoption from physicians.”
Lecun and Lebrun, who both hail from France, worked together at the Facebook AI Research lab, or FAIR, in Paris. Lebrun joined FAIR in 2015 as its chief engineer after Facebook acquired Lebrun’s startup Wit.ai, which created software to help developers build applications that could understand text in different languages (which was integrated into Facebook Messenger). Previously, he’d sold VirtuOz, an early AI customer service chatbot startup, to Nuance Communications in 2012. (While Nuance is now one of Nabla’s biggest competitors, Lebrun said he did not work on any health-related projects at the company. He declined to disclose the acquisition prices of either company.)
At FAIR, Lebrun worked on Facebook M, a now defunct project that tried to blend AI models and human concierges to do things like book a rental car reservation. It was some of the early work on what we now know as large language models. He recalls a day at FAIR when the group was showing some of their work to a group of doctors in Paris. “This kind of automation, if you can adapt this to medicine, would be a game changer for us and for our patients,” he remembers them saying.
In 2018, he left FAIR and assembled a team — including CTO Martin Raison, a cofounder of Wit.ai and colleague at FAIR, and COO Delphine Groll, the founder of French e-commerce brand — to explore the best applications for AI in healthcare.
Nabla took a unique approach to product development. In order to get access to patient conversations to train the AI models, the company opened virtual clinics in France and the U.K. and recorded 30,000 patient visits over two years. Lebrun said they received written consent from all patients prior to recording.
Since the launch of its automated medical note-taking software last year, the company is using a marketing and sales strategy that has more in common with tech companies like Slack and Dropbox, rather than the typical healthcare approach that relies on a large sales team. Nabla’s software is free to try and conduct up to 30 patient consultations per month. After that, it’s $119 per month for an individual membership. “It's bottom up sales,” Lebrun said. “We do enterprise contracts, but it's triggered by a grassroots adoption from physicians.”
Lebrun said this quarter Nabla plans to launch services that help clinics automatically generate the codes that are needed to bill insurance companies for particular medical services. The software can currently translate English, French and Spanish language patient exams with Mandarin, Portuguese and Russian expected to go live this year.
One of the other areas where he sees Nabla having a leg up is data privacy. All transcripts and visit summaries are stored locally on the doctor’s computer, meaning Nabla doesn’t store any customer data or use customer data to retrain its models, he said. (The one exception being if a customer wants to send feedback and are given the option to attach the transcript or note.) Unlike some competitors, Lebrun said, “When you finish your consultation, we forget everything about you.”

title: Council Post: AI And The Next “Aha” Moment
text:
Oleg is the CEO of dxFeed, a market data and financial services firm. Over 20 years of experience in information technology and finance.
In 2023, we saw AI burst onto the main stage like never before. The promise of intelligent machines has been one of our most enduring technological ambitions, but 2023 saw AI move from the realms of scientific speculation to a fact of life that suddenly everyone has to contend with. What's next for 2024?
How We Got Here
Besides the public experimentation taking place with these new generative AI tools, there’s a deeper acceptance that something genuinely more impactful than a productivity tool has arrived. This is perhaps the greatest shift in public perception, and it may end up marking what this period will be remembered for in the future. For example, most of us have already been forced to take stock of how AI could affect our respective businesses.
We also saw this acceptance reflected in the way AI rapidly became the dominant market theme for most of the year, with AI-related stocks buoying the performance of major indices such as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 amidst major macroeconomic headwinds and geopolitical turmoil. This was no mean feat for what remains the speculative end of an already speculative tech sector. It was as if in 2023 it suddenly dawned on investors en masse that this was not a technology to short, macro be damned.
This shift in consensus may not seem like much of a big deal, but that’s only because we’ve so rapidly come to take it for granted. In 2013, a sci-fi film like Her, which details a love affair between a lonely man and his AI assistant, seemed far-fetched. But in 2023 and 2024, AI companions are available via subscription model and many of us can already report interactions with AI that took unexpected turns. That’s just ten years for science fiction to start looking much more like science fact.
How We Make it Better
A generation ago, search revolutionized how we browse the web. Without it, the deluge of data being uploaded to the internet each day would’ve been impossible to navigate.
Today, we’re confronted with the next version of this problem. And now it’s not just about static websites. The task is to make sense of a universe of ceaseless real-time data detailing everything from the oscillations of capital markets to the habits, preferences and movements of almost 8 billion people. I believe AI holds the promise of becoming our primary digital sense-making tool, just like how Google became the ubiquitous search tool.
Even in its current iteration, ChatGPT does a better job for most users in providing concise, reliable answers to general search queries than those users could have gleaned for themselves by googling. Current Large Language Models are already capable generalists, just by having access to the web content included in their training data.
What needs to happen now, and indeed what is happening, is that these models are being transformed from generalists into experts across a myriad of fields by receiving training on much higher-quality data. I believe this will lead to an explosion in domain-specific AIs, such as those that specialize in accounting practices, legal systems, academic scholarship, medical records, capital markets and much more.
In a modern twist to the old Einstein quote about not understanding something if you can’t explain it simply, we’re about to find out which players are the real experts in a variety of fields, by virtue of which datasets prove the most impactful in training the next generation of AI systems.
AI In The Workplace
In my own company's experiments, we’ve already been able to greatly improve ChatGPT’s proficiency with market-related queries. When trained on our proprietary market data, the model provides accurate answers to real-time price queries, performs analysis and provides summaries of recent activity pertaining to individual symbols, asset classes and even prominent figures such as company CEOs and central bankers.
This is why I and my team anticipate that the next real "aha" moment for the general public regarding these technologies may very well be in the workplace. This is where people are most likely to witness just how powerful these systems can be when trained on the appropriate data. For this reason, we also anticipate that these sources of proprietary data will initially remain siloed as sector leaders begin to recognize the true value of their data and attempt to extract value from it.
This will take many forms, from AIs created specifically for internal purposes to confer competitive advantages, to AIs that offer access to an entity’s accumulated knowledge as a service, and eventually M&A activity that will bring that siloed data together in more general AI instantiations.
Artificial General Intelligence
OpenAI's recent unveiling of its "Q*" model represents a pivotal advancement in the quest for Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). This development is a game-changer, showcasing an ability to grasp and execute a diverse array of complex tasks, thus moving closer to the elusive goal of AGI.
For the software development industry, this innovation heralds a transformative era. It suggests the emergence of more intuitive programming tools, the streamlining of the coding process and the potential automation of certain intricacies of software engineering.
In finance, the impact is equally groundbreaking. The model's superior learning and data-processing capabilities could significantly refine the accuracy of market analyses, risk evaluations and investment strategies.
In Conclusion
While 2023 proved to be a massive "aha" moment for investors in this technology and prospective users alike, ultimately, the "aha" moments regarding the power and utility of these models have only just begun.
The next milestones will require vision and concentrated effort from the leaders in various sectors to begin reimagining how the data their respective businesses generate can be utilized in this new age of AI.

title: Council Post: AI And Personalization In Marketing
text:
Alan VP of Marketing at Jafton.
AI's integration across sectors, especially marketing, is revolutionizing innovation, emphasizing efficiency and adaptability. Brands now leverage AI to foster deeper, personalized connections with audiences, transforming customer engagement.
Personalization in marketing is paramount. Today's tech-savvy consumers demand unique experiences, making generic campaigns obsolete. AI, analyzing extensive data, pioneers this shift toward hyper-personalized marketing to redefine global marketing strategies.
For marketers and entrepreneurs alike, I believe grasping the interplay between AI and personalization is important for contemporary success.
Understanding AI-Driven Personalization: Background And Benefits
In pre-digital times, marketing personalization was manual, based on broad demographics and direct feedback, and often lacking accuracy. The digital revolution brought an influx of consumer data, but despite early algorithms, genuine personalization was challenging.
The advent of AI and machine learning revolutionized this. Marketers shifted from broad categorizations to focusing on individual behaviors, transitioning from reactive to anticipatory strategies. Essentially, the move from intuition to AI-driven methods underscores technology's transformative role in contemporary marketing.
At its core, AI-driven personalization leverages AI to tailor marketing efforts to individual consumers. It goes beyond traditional data analytics by using machine learning algorithms to predict and adapt to user behaviors in real time.
AI systems process extensive data from sources like browsing histories, purchase records and social media. Take a user interested in athletic wear who recently ran a marathon, for example. AI could merge this data with their social media activity to recommend specific running gear.
Through analyzing such data, AI identifies unique user patterns. As it gathers more data, its understanding sharpens, making its predictions more accurate. This continuous adaptation distinguishes AI-driven personalization from conventional methods. Potential benefits of this approach include:
Enhanced Customer Experience
AI's ability to predict and understand customer preferences in real time ensures that consumers receive content and offers that resonate deeply with their individual needs and desires.
Increased ROI
With more precise targeting, businesses can achieve better conversion rates and customer retention, leading to improved return on investment.
Scalability
AI can handle vast amounts of data, allowing brands to provide personalization at scale, reaching vast audiences with tailored content.
Real-Time Decision Making
AI's capability to make instantaneous decisions based on real-time data ensures that marketing efforts are timely and relevant.
In essence, AI-driven personalization is about harnessing the power of technology to understand and cater to the nuances of individual consumer behavior, making marketing efforts more relevant and effective.
Real-World Applications, Challenges And Considerations
The transformative power of AI-driven personalization is evident in various sectors, reshaping how businesses interact with their consumers. For example, platforms like Amazon utilize AI to suggest products tailored to individual browsing and purchase histories. Streaming services like Netflix or Spotify employ AI to curate content based on user preferences, ensuring that recommendations align with individual tastes. Even AI-driven chatbots provide personalized solutions to customer queries, often predicting needs based on past interactions and preferences.
Data Privacy Concerns
However, with these advancements come challenges. As AI systems rely heavily on user data, there's a fine line between personalization and privacy invasion. Brands must ensure they adhere to data protection regulations and prioritize user consent.
Here are some examples of how companies can adhere to data protection regulations and prioritize user consent in the context of AI systems. One effective approach for brands to consider is the implementation of a comprehensive and transparent data privacy framework:
1. Developing A Clear Data Privacy Policy: This policy should be easily accessible and understandable by users. It must clearly outline what data is collected, how it is used and the steps taken to protect it.
2. User Consent Management: Implement a robust system for obtaining and managing user consent. This includes clear options for users to opt in or out of data collection, with mechanisms that are easy to use and understand.
3. Regular Audits And Compliance Checks: Conduct regular audits to ensure compliance with all relevant data protection regulations (like GDPR, CCPA, etc.). This also involves staying updated with any changes in these laws and adjusting practices accordingly.
4. Investing In Data Security Technologies: Utilize state-of-the-art security technologies to safeguard user data. This includes encryption, secure data storage solutions and regular security assessments.
5. Educating And Training Staff: Ensure all employees are well-versed in data privacy practices and understand the importance of adhering to these policies. Regular training sessions can be beneficial.
6. Transparent Communication With Users: Keep users informed about how their data is being used and any changes in the privacy policy. Transparency builds trust and shows a commitment to protecting user data.
7. Leveraging Privacy-Enhancing Technologies: Use technologies like anonymization, pseudonymization and differential privacy to minimize the risk of data misuse while still deriving valuable insights.
8. User-Centric Design: Design AI systems with user privacy in mind from the outset. This involves considering the implications of data collection and processing on user privacy during the system design phase.
By following these steps, brands can adhere to data protection regulations while demonstrating a commitment to respecting user privacy, enhancing reputation and user trust.
Over-Reliance On AI
While AI offers precision, there's a risk of losing the human touch. Striking a balance between automation and human interaction in marketing, especially when using AI, is crucial to avoid this issue. One strategy I've found effective is a "hybrid marketing model." Here's how this can be approached:
1. Defining Roles For AI And Human Interaction: Delineate the tasks best suited for AI and those that require human intervention. AI is excellent for data analysis, predictive modeling and automation of repetitive tasks, while human expertise is essential for creative content creation, strategy development and nuanced customer service.
2. Personalizing With AI, Engaging With Humans: Use AI to gather insights and personalize marketing efforts, such as targeted advertisements and customized content. However, ensure that human teams are involved in engaging with customers, especially in responding to queries, complaints and feedback.
3. Training And Upskilling Teams: Invest in training marketing teams to work alongside AI. This includes understanding how to interpret AI-generated data and insights and how to apply them in a human-centric way.
4. Feedback Loops: Establish feedback loops where human insights can inform and refine AI algorithms. This helps avoid biases and ensures AI-driven marketing remains relevant and sensitive to customer needs.
5. Ethical And Empathetic Marketing: Embed ethical considerations and empathy in marketing strategies. AI should be used to enhance the customer experience, not manipulate it. Human oversight is key in ensuring the ethical use of data.
6. Augmentation, Not Replacement: Position AI as a tool to augment human capabilities, not replace them. This perspective helps in leveraging AI for efficiency while retaining the human elements that are crucial for brand identity and customer relationships.
7. Experiment And Iterate: Experiment with different blends of AI and human interaction. Iteratively improve based on results and customer feedback. This adaptive approach allows brands to find the right balance unique to their market and audience.
Conclusion
AI-driven personalization is reshaping marketing, offering unparalleled insights and engagement opportunities with consumers. Its potential is vast, but businesses must balance technological innovation with transparency and ethics.
The future of marketing hinges on not just advanced algorithms but also on genuine connections with consumers. In this evolving landscape, brands that merge AI capabilities with human values can work toward setting the gold standard in personalized marketing, ensuring relevance and trust in every interaction.

title: Council Post: Yet Another 2024 Digital Marketing Forecast
text:
Tom Wozniak heads up Marketing and Communications as the COO for OPTIZMO Technologies.
’Tis the season … for pundits and marketing industry experts to come out with lots of forecasts and predictions for 2024. Far be it for me to skip out on the annual exercise, so here is my take on some larger trends in the digital marketing industry over the coming year and tips on how marketers can take advantage of or adapt to the changes. I decided to focus on three main areas where I anticipate a lot happening that will impact marketers regularly.
AI Takes The Next Step
It’s pretty safe to say that AI will evolve and be a key driver of change for marketers in 2024, but here are three particular things to watch out for.
Next-Gen…erative AI: All the 2023 experimentation with ChatGPT and Bard will lead to some real advancements. All those people kicking the tires on generative AI and prompting it to answer questions or create a wide variety of content have helped AI companies push their tools forward. Expect them to leap forward in the ability to tailor responses to the users more easily.
Individualized AI Assistants: Users will be able to train their AI iteration so that they can learn how to deliver the right content, written in the company’s voice and also take on other tasks. The concept of a highly functional AI assistant is right around the corner, helping with various routine tasks like scheduling.
AI Costs Increase: Well we all knew that the era of nearly free AI tools had to come to an end eventually. So, expect AI companies to start charging higher costs to use their platforms, as they begin to shift from beta mode to becoming profitable businesses.
As marketers, 2024 will be a time to more critically examine the value proposition for AI in all facets of the marketing operation. Look for ways to leverage evolving capabilities in content creation and more operational areas, but start taking current and future costs into account as you plan for the future.
Regulatory Changes Keep Coming
If there’s any topic as easy to forecast as the continued evolution of AI, it’s the enactment of more laws and regulations in the U.S. and abroad that will impact marketers’ day to day. Here are just a few to expect.
Lead Generation Opt-Ins: In December, the FCC is expected to vote on a new rule related to how marketers can collect and leverage consumer leads, particularly via text and calls. I won’t get into the legal weeds (since I am not an attorney) but the gist is that lead generation companies were previously able to collect a lead and essentially opt that consumer into receiving communications from a wide variety of brands. Under the proposed rule, one-to-one consent would need to be acquired for each brand.
Data Privacy: It’s safe to say that there will be more state-level data privacy laws passed in the U.S. in 2024. But will there be a federal data privacy law passed to standard the rules across the nation? The time feels about right for a federal standard, and the currently fractured environment of state-level regulations will become more difficult for marketers to navigate. However, with a divided Congress in an election year, I won’t be surprised if this doesn’t take priority and we have to wait another year for something to pass at the federal level.
AI Regulation: The question isn’t if more AI regulation will pass in the U.S. and around the world, but whether it will be written in a way that impacts the industry in a meaningful way. Regulating an industry that is evolving at lightning speed isn’t easy. Add to that an industry that is hard for most people to truly comprehend, and it becomes exponentially more difficult. More regulations will be enacted, but they likely won’t slow the industry’s progress.
If you haven’t focused much on regulatory or legal changes in the past, it’s time to get up to speed. Always rely on professional legal advice, but don’t let that stop you from learning all you can about these regulations yourself.
Marketing Platforms Will Evolve
Now let’s get a little more speculative. Marketing platforms and channels are always evolving, but it’s not often that one of the largest and most well-known platforms is at risk of losing its position.
Gmail and Yahoo: The two biggest email inbox providers recently got together and announced several requirements they will impose on large email marketers beginning in February of 2024. The changes will require large-scale mailers to adopt a set of best practices involving one-click list-header unsubscribe options, adoption of various email authentication protocols and processing opt-out requests even faster (two days) than legally required in the U.S. (10 business days).
X Marks the Spot: But, will it still be relevant or viable for brands by the end of 2024? We have all been watching as X (formerly known as Twitter) has gone through a lot of upheaval over the last year. Various brands and agencies have either scaled back or taken a wait-and-see approach to long-term plans to market on the platform. No competing platform (Threads, etc.) has gained enough traction to replace X from the standpoint of reach, but brands want to feel comfortable that their ads won’t show up next to questionable content. We may already be seeing an inflection point where brands decide the risk-reward relationship is no longer in their favor when advertising on the platform.
Be prepared for potentially significant changes to platforms you have been using for a while. I didn’t mention it above, but AdSense is making potentially impactful changes to how it pays publishers (shifting from paying per click to paying per impression). The point is that you should be closely monitoring changes in the platforms you already use, along with others that might come into play for you in 2024.

title: Council Post: Why Cybersecurity Is Foundational To AI Safety
text:
Marcus Fowler is SVP of Strategic Engagements and Threats at Darktrace and CEO of Darktrace Federal.
From smartphones and social media to the internet itself, technology has the power to fundamentally change our daily lives. But too often technology’s rapid development and adoption outpaces our ability to discuss their associated risks. While the benefits of these advancements are great, there are often unintended consequences with lasting effects.
With generative AI such as ChatGPT becoming widely available, AI has seen a rapid rise in public adoption across industry verticals. This new generation of AI marks a technological advancement that is potentially on par with the introduction of the internet but with adoption orders of magnitude faster. The potential benefits are vast; however, we’re already seeing early signs of how this technology could be misused and threats that could derail its potential. For example, deepfakes are being used to spread misinformation, and sophisticated novel social engineering attacks are crafted using generative AI.
Global Initiatives: Addressing AI Safety And Security
Fortunately, the global community has demonstrated a strong commitment to moving quickly to address the potential risks. The U.K. hosted the inaugural AI Safety Summit in early November. In the same week, the Biden-Harris Administration released an executive order establishing new standards for AI safety and security. Both countries have announced new AI Safety Institutes to develop robust techniques to evaluate AI. Most recently, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) collaborated on guidelines for building secure AI systems, which have been adopted by 21 other international agencies.
As AI becomes embedded into the tools and processes we depend on every day, it is vital that they are secure. In fact, the Biden-Harris Administration’s executive order highlights cybersecurity as a significant risk to AI systems. Cybersecurity is foundational to AI safety—it is a prerequisite for trustworthy and safe AI.
To realize the importance of prioritizing cybersecurity, it’s helpful to understand the cyber risks to AI safety: offensive applications of AI in cyberspace, accidental insider threats and cyberattacks targeting AI itself.
At Darktrace, we have been researching offensive applications of AI in cyberspace for years. The rise of generative AI is lowering barriers for attackers and is poised to make them faster. AI-powered cyberattacks can involve using large language models (LLM) to generate sophisticated or highly personalized text in phishing emails, and this process can be completely automated using tools like AutoGPT. LLMs are already showing up on the dark web that claim to write malware code for a few hundred dollars, and attackers can use AI to augment nearly every stage of the attack lifecycle from reconnaissance to command and control.
It’s not just attackers who are using AI to drive more efficiency. AI tools have been rapidly adopted by companies and workers: As of June 2023, we saw that nearly 75% of our customers already had some employees using generative AI tools. However, well-intentioned employees run the risk of inadvertent misuse. For example, an employee inserting sensitive data into a prompt-based LLM tool such as ChatGPT might unintentionally leak proprietary or personal data.
In a high-profile incident, these concerns motivated the U.S. Space Force to temporarily ban Guardians from using government data in generative AI solutions, with a Space Force spokesperson citing the need to "ensure that sensitive DOD data is safeguarded when using such platforms."
It is also important to protect AI systems themselves against cyberattacks. Take, for example, the secure development of AI. This involves defending against threats such as "data poisoning" attacks that corrupt training data to adversely affect the AI’s behavior. Attacks like these may cause the AI to behave in ways that are unexpected or harmful. As AI gets embedded into critical infrastructure and business processes, it’s critical that attackers can’t hijack or trick the guardrails within these tools. Cyberattacks can also be used to steal intellectual property (IP), not only for AI algorithms and data but also for advanced chips that drive AI development.
Priorities: Data Privacy, Control And Trust
It’s positive to see governments taking action to predict the challenges this new generation of general-purpose AI presents. Our history of predicting or properly securing and overseeing technologies, such as the internet and social media adoption, is inadequate, and we can see how much more difficult it is to put the genie back in the bottle. There are three areas of action that governments and companies should prioritize: data privacy, control and trust.
AI systems should be privacy-preserving. Companies building and using general-purpose AI need to protect the data they collect and use to train their models. Organizations should invest in safeguards to detect, identify and test potential risks that can come from within their businesses. That means guarding against personally protected information accidentally being leaked through prompt injections on generative AI platforms.
Humans need control, particularly as general-purpose AI tools become increasingly relied on to take real-world actions. It’s critical to apply cybersecurity best practices to protect models and invest in safeguards to keep AI systems protected at all stages of the AI lifecycle to avoid unintended behaviors or potential hijacking of the algorithms.
Security and transparency are always the foundation of trust: If people cannot have faith in the cybersecurity of their AI systems, they will not be able to trust them to carry out critical functions. Developers can help to ensure that people understand and are aware of how an AI system reaches its decisions and answers.
Though the AI safety risks posed by malicious cyber activity are serious, there is no reason to fall into pessimism. Instead, one should feel optimistic to see the proactive measures taken by the global community. Agencies across the U.S. Federal Government are already working to implement the executive order, and South Korea and France are working on a second and third Global AI Safety Summit.
The good news is that tried-and-true AI tools already exist for cyber defense and have been defending critical infrastructure and other sensitive environments for over a decade. Cybersecurity is foundational to AI safety, and AI itself can play a vital role in mitigating risks.

text:

US regulator denies Apple, Disney bids to skip votes on AI
Corporations have embraced the new technology for its promised efficiencies. But the trend has prompted fears it would replace many creative and professional workers or unfairly draw on their work, issues in recent Hollywood labor disputes and a recent New York Times lawsuit. But the trend has prompted fears it would replace many creative and professional workers or unfairly draw on their work, issues in recent Hollywood labor disputes and a recent New York Times lawsuit.
Apple and Disney cannot avoid shareholder votes about their use of artificial intelligence put forward by a labor group, the top US securities regulator has ruled.
In notices dated January 3, the US Securities and Exchange Commission rejected requests by the iPhone maker and by the entertainment giant to exclude from their upcoming annual meetings calls for reports on their use of AI.
Corporations have embraced the new technology for its promised efficiencies. But the trend has prompted fears it would replace many creative and professional workers or unfairly draw on their work, issues in recent Hollywood labor disputes and a recent New York Times lawsuit.
The similar shareholder proposals were filed by a pension trust of the AFL-CIO, the largest American labor union federation, which also has AI measures pending at four other technology companies.
At Apple, the group asked for a report on the company's use of AI "in its business operations and disclose any ethical guidelines that the company has adopted regarding the company's use of AI technology." In a similar request, it also asked Disney to report on its board's role overseeing AI usage.
In its supporting statement at Apple the AFL-CIO wrote that "AI systems should not be trained on copyrighted works, or the voices, likenesses and performances of professional performers, without transparency, consent and compensation to creators and rights holders."
Brandon Rees, deputy director of the AFL-CIO's office of investment, said the SEC's decisions could pave the way for agreements with Apple and Disney that would only bring them into line with the AI disclosures of other companies like Microsoft .
Apple and Disney, in contrast, "haven't even begun to grapple with these ethical issues" around AI, Rees said.
Apple and Disney did not immediately responded to requests for comment.
Both companies had argued the proposals could be left off their ballots because they related to "ordinary business operations," such as the company's choice of technologies.
The SEC disagreed. "In our view, the Proposal transcends ordinary business matters and does not seek to micromanage the Company," the agency wrote in separate letters.

title: How an AI robot smashed human world record in Labyrinth, a classic marble maze game
text:
You’ve probably heard of AI winning against humans in games like chess and GO that require intellect. That’s impressive but not shocking.
AI is good at crunching numbers and finding patterns.
But what about physical skills? That’s something humans are supposed to be better at, right? Well, not anymore.
An AI labyrinth maze champion emerges
Researchers at ETH Zurich have created an AI robot with the task of learning how to play the popular wooden labyrinth maze game. The goal of the game is simple, using two knobs, you have to steer a marble ball from a start to an endpoint without it falling into the holes across the board. But if you’ve ever played it, you know it’s actually easier said than done. The scientific explanation behind its difficulty is that it requires acute motor skills, spatial reasoning abilities — and a lot of practice.
WHAT IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)?
MORE: HOW THIS ROBOT HELPS YOU PROTECT AND CONNECT YOUR HOME
Meet the new robot champion
The robot, named CyberRunner, is equipped with two motors (its hands), a camera (its eyes), and a computer (its brain), allowing it to play the game just like a person would. Much like a human, CyberRunner learns through experience by leveraging recent advances in model-based reinforcement learning, which enables the AI to make decisions and choose potential successful behaviors by predicting the outcomes of different courses of action.
While playing the game, CyberRunner makes observations of the labyrinth and receives rewards based on its performance. It keeps a memory of the collected experience, or as we humans call it, "practice," which the algorithm uses to learn how the system behaves.

Based on this knowledge, it’s able to recognize the most promising behaviors. As a result, the robot’s use of the two motors continuously improves, and CyberRunner keeps getting better while the algorithm runs every time it plays.
MORE: HUMANOID ROBOTS ARE NOW DOING THE WORK OF HUMANS IN A SPANX WAREHOUSE
The triumph of the robot in breaking the human record
The robot received 6.06 hours of practice. Impressively, it beat the previous world record set by Lars Göran Danielsson, who set a time of 15.41 seconds in 2022. CyberRunner completed the game in 14.48 seconds — faster by over 6% compared to the human record holder.
During the learning process, the researchers say the robot discovered shortcuts and found ways to cheat — a behavior that they are studying as an innate human trait. Therefore, the researchers had to step in and instruct CyberRunner not to skip parts of the maze.
MORE: THE NEXT GENERATION OF TESLA'S HUMANOID ROBOT MAKES ITS DEBUT
What can be learned from CyberRunner?
Researchers Thomas Bi and Raffaello D’Andrea are making available the robotic system's hardware and software open-source so that others can benefit and learn from their breakthrough in AI skill acquisition. They want to spur other scientists and engineers to use their experiment as an opportunity to conduct their own research. For those interested, their research paper is available here.
Kurt's key takeaways
CyberRunner's victory marks a significant milestone in the field of artificial intelligence, demonstrating that AI can now outperform humans not only in tasks that involve information processing but also in physical skill games. The project's open-source approach ensures that the benefits of this achievement are accessible to a wider audience, paving the way for further innovations in real-world machine learning and AI. As we witness AI breaking new ground, the line between human and machine capabilities continues to blur.
